Then there’s Saturn’s moon, Enceladus, which also has geysers shooting water into space. The fact that these moons might have subsurface oceans opens up all kinds of possibilities. Who knows what kind of microbial life could be swimming around in those alien waters?

On the flip side, the inner solar system's planets don’t have many moons (poor Mars has just two tiny ones!). This makes the outer solar system much more diverse in terms of potential habitats. While the rocky inner planets are interesting, the icy and gaseous worlds of the outer solar system present unique environments that might be suitable for life—albeit very different from what we know on Earth.

In summary, the outer solar system offers a stark contrast to its inner counterpart. With gas giants and icy moons, the conditions are vastly different, shaping the kinds of environments that might support life. While Earth is our best example of a life-supporting planet, we’re starting to realize that we might not be alone in the cosmos after all.
